newsitem.title: UK: Trusty soapbox is Major's secret election weapon.
newsitem.headline: Trusty soapbox is Major's secret election weapon.

text.p: In the long, gruelling battle that is Britain's election campaign, Prime Minister John Major has a secret weapon that he hopes will turn his Conservative Party from political underdogs into winners.
Like Major, presented as "honest John" in the dirty world of British politics, it's slightly the worse for wear and looks more at home in the 1950s than at the brink of the 21st century.

But no sooner had Major announced the May 1 election date than he had pulled out the battered wooden packing case he used as a soapbox to clinch a surprise victory in the last election five years ago.

Major took his trusty ally, patched up with parcel tape, to the streets of working-class Luton to meet the noisy, real people excluded from the slick world of political advertising and the comfortable sofas of television interview studios.
It was here, in the same bleak town north of London in 1992, that Major first got up on his soapbox to make himself heard to to heckling crowds during a walkabout.
Major compared the event to his days in his thirties as a local councillor in south London when he shouted Conservative policies from a soapbox.
The move was derided by some in his party as old-fashioned and un-prime ministerial but the critics proved to be wrong.

Major's soapbox electioneering style of a pre-television era proved a news story in itself and became a symbol of the Conservative comeback which overturned a Labour lead in opinion polls and won the Conservatives a fourth consecutive term.

Armed only with a cheap stand-up microphone to make himself heard above the largely hostile crowds, Major on Monday set the style of a campaign that this time sees the Conservatives starting some 25 points behind Labour in polls.
Major says he relishes getting out of London and meeting people during the campaign.

"Elections, some people say, are tough and gruelling businesses. Well, up to a point that's true. I think they are also a lot of fun and I am looking forward to going up and down the country taking the message that I believe is right for this country to everyone," he told a news conference.
Despite being attacked for weak leadership and a lack of charisma, Major is seen as the best asset in a Conservative Party riven by splits over Europe and allegations of sleaze.
Major may appear dull and ordinary but he is also seen as trustworthy and a man with the common touch -- a strong contrast to the slick, media-savvy leader of "New" Labour, Tony Blair.
